title: The Abandoned Order
gist: Mark Leonard argues the world has entered a 'rotten-tail' era of un-order — not a transition from a U.S.-led to a Chinese-led system but the absence of any order at all — driven by fragmentation, contagion, and the weaponization of chokepoints (energy, chips, dollar, food), and urges former U.S. allies to abandon 'architect' thinking (grand multilateral blueprints) for 'artisan' improvisation: flexible coalitions, self-reliance, and defensive chokepoint leverage of their own.

themes.theme: The central metaphor and thesis: a 'rotten-tail' world

insights.claim: The U.S.-led rules-based international order is being abandoned much like China's crashed housing market left thousands of unfinished 'rotten-tail' (lanwei lou) apartment buildings — never fully accepted by China or Russia, resented by rising middle powers, and now abandoned even by its main financial backer, the American public, with no alternative provider stepping in to complete it.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: Sets the article's central framework: states must adapt by improvising with the remnants of the old order rather than waiting for it to be rebuilt or replaced by a Chinese-led alternative.
insights.quote: The state of the Chinese housing market is a good metaphor for the U.S.-led rules-based international order. After decades of expansion, it, too, is being abandoned.

insights.claim: The current moment is not a short interregnum between a U.S.-led order and a Chinese-led one; for the foreseeable future the world will have no order at all, swept by fragmentation, contagion, and the strangulation of chokepoints.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: Explicitly rejects the 'multipolar transition to Chinese hegemony' narrative in favor of a genuine order vacuum — a materially different scenario for long-horizon geopolitical risk pricing than a simple US-to-China power transfer.
insights.quote: This moment does not constitute a short interregnum between a U.S.-led order and a Chinese-led one. For some time, the world will be without any order at all

insights.claim: Both pillars of world order that Henry Kissinger identified — a reasonably stable balance of power and a set of commonly agreed rules — are crumbling and unlikely to be fortified or rebuilt any time soon, evidenced by the fact that Washington could not even reopen the Strait of Hormuz after a militarily hobbled Iran shuttered it.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: Uses the Hormuz episode as concrete proof that U.S. military primacy no longer guarantees the ability to enforce open commerce, a direct signal for repricing energy-chokepoint risk premiums.
insights.quote: But it is increasingly clear that Washington no longer has the ability to prevent conflicts or ensure the free flow of commerce worldwide; it could not even open the Strait of Hormuz after a militarily hobbled Iran shuttered the waterway.

themes.theme: Allies in denial about U.S. withdrawal

insights.claim: At the July 2026 NATO summit, European leaders pledged arbitrary defense-spending increases unrelated to their own defense analysts' assessments purely to appease Trump, while the UK kept buying U.S. fighter jets and Denmark approved major U.S. arms purchases even as Trump threatened to forcibly annex Denmark's Greenland.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: A vivid, dated (July 2026) example of allied cognitive dissonance — continuing to deepen U.S. defense dependence even while the U.S. threatens one member's sovereign territory — illustrating the gap between rhetoric and hedging behavior worth tracking in European defense procurement decisions.
insights.quote: NATO’s July 2026 summit offered one of the most surreal examples of cognitive dissonance: European leaders frenetically pledged tributes to U.S. President Donald Trump in the form of arbitrary defense spending increases—unrelated to their own defense analysts’ assessments—in the hope that he would not withdraw from the alliance.

themes.theme: Fragmentation: no shared facts, no shared markets

insights.claim: The deepest fragmentation is epistemic: a digitally connected world no longer agrees on basic facts, erasing the shared reality that underpins diplomacy — illustrated by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, where the parties couldn't even agree on whether a cease-fire existed or who had won.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: Identifies a new, harder-to-fix category of fragmentation (disagreement over facts, not just interpretations) that undermines the basic preconditions for diplomacy and cease-fire verification — relevant to assessing the durability of any future negotiated settlements.
insights.quote: A digitally connected world is not simply dividing over interpretations; its inhabitants no longer agree on facts, erasing the sense of shared reality that underpins diplomacy itself. Consider the war that the United States and Israel launched against Iran in February. The parties to the conflict have been unable even to agree on whether a cease-fire exists

insights.claim: In early April 2026, Brent oil futures traded at around $113 per barrel while physical cargoes of the same commodity sold for as much as $144 — an unusually wide spread reflecting fragmented pricing by payment system, sanctions regime, and buyer, with similar divergence appearing in the London and New York gold markets.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: A concrete, sourced data point showing physical commodity markets are fragmenting from futures markets to a historically unusual degree — directly relevant for commodity traders and anyone pricing sanctions-driven basis risk in oil and gold.
insights.quote: In early April, for instance, Brent futures traded at around $113 per barrel while physical cargoes of the stuff sold for as much as $144 per barrel. Oil futures and spot prices usually diverge, but only by a few dollars; such a spread is extremely unusual.

insights.claim: The dollar's dominance will erode more rapidly, with its share of global foreign exchange reserves perhaps falling below 50 percent as bilateral currency arrangements proliferate and commodity pricing diversifies, while U.S. borrowing costs rise and global transaction costs balloon as incompatible payment systems multiply.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: A specific, falsifiable forecast (dollar reserve share below 50%) directly relevant to currency-reserve allocation, de-dollarization trades, and long-term U.S. Treasury yield forecasting.
insights.quote: The dollar’s dominance will erode more rapidly, with its share of global foreign exchange reserves perhaps falling below 50 percent as bilateral currency arrangements proliferate and the pricing of commodities diversifies. U.S. borrowing costs will rise

themes.theme: Contagion: crises no longer stay contained, war norms are eroding

insights.claim: Unlike in 2003, when France and Germany opposed the Iraq War but kept sharing intelligence and trading with Washington, Trump's threatened tariffs against European allies over the Greenland claim and his threats during the Iran war to halt trade with dissenting European states and withdraw troops show that economic and security relations are no longer compartmentalized even among allies.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: Documents a structural break from historical alliance norms (compartmentalized disagreement) toward cross-domain retaliation, meaning trade and security disputes can no longer be assumed to stay contained even between formal allies.
insights.quote: When Trump threatened tariffs against European allies who opposed his claim to Greenland, by contrast, he demonstrated that even among allies, economic and security relations are no longer separate. During the recent Iran war, when several European countries expressed reservations about the conflict, Trump threatened to halt trade with them and withdraw troops stationed in their countries.

insights.claim: After Israel and the United States attacked Iran, Iran and its proxies struck U.S. partners Bahrain, Oman, Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, the UAE, and even Cyprus, while the UAE retaliated against Pakistan for its closeness to Iran by forcing early repayment of a $3.5 billion debt and deporting thousands of Pakistani workers.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence of conflict contagion spreading across theaters via economic coercion (a $3.5B debt call and mass deportations), illustrating how a Middle East war can rapidly generate financial and labor-market shocks in unrelated countries like Pakistan.
insights.quote: Frustrated by Pakistan’s closeness to Iran, the United Arab Emirates, for its part, also retaliated across domains by forcing an early repayment of a $3.5 billion debt and deporting thousands of Pakistani workers.

insights.claim: Traditional wartime taboos against assassination, targeting civilians, and territorial conquest are vanishing: according to The New York Times, Israel planned to assassinate the Iranian foreign minister and parliament speaker during negotiations with the U.S., while Israel has struck journalists, hospitals, and cultural sites in Gaza, and Russia and Ukraine conduct targeted assassinations of each other's citizens in third countries.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: Documents the erosion of century-old wartime conduct norms with specific, sourced examples — a leading indicator of rising escalation risk and reduced predictability in ongoing and future conflicts.
insights.quote: According to reporting in The New York Times, Israel planned to assassinate the Iranian foreign minister and speaker of parliament while the two were conducting negotiations with the United States.

insights.claim: Under conditions of disinhibited great-power behavior, the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty could cease to function as a meaningful constraint, with Germany, Iran, Poland, Saudi Arabia, and South Korea potentially moving to acquire nuclear weapons within two decades.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: Names five specific candidate countries for nuclear proliferation within a 20-year window — a concrete watchlist for nuclear-proliferation and regional-security risk tracking.
insights.quote: The Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty could cease to function as a meaningful constraint, and Germany, Iran, Poland, Saudi Arabia, and South Korea could move to acquire nuclear weapons within two decades.

insights.claim: Possible catalysts for a proliferation of small territorial wars include China targeting Taiwan outright, Venezuela using force to pursue its claim on Guyana's resource-rich Essequibo region, Ethiopia trying to seize access to Eritrea's Red Sea ports, and Russia seizing the Estonian border town of Narva.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: A specific, named watchlist of four potential territorial-conquest flashpoints (Taiwan, Essequibo, Eritrea's ports, Narva) for geopolitical-risk monitoring and tail-risk hedging.
insights.quote: China could target Taiwan outright; Venezuela could decide to use force in pursuit of its claim on Essequibo, the resource-rich western half of neighboring Guyana; Ethiopia might try to wrest access to Eritrea’s Red Sea ports; and Russia might decide to seize the Estonian border town of Narva.

insights.claim: In late 2025, China adopted its own version of the U.S. foreign direct product rule, asserting the right to decide whether companies anywhere in the world can access magnets that contain even trace amounts of Chinese materials or were made using Chinese technology — turning the extraterritorial tactic Washington invented for chips against Washington itself.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: Documents a specific, dated (late 2025) escalation in China's extraterritorial control over rare-earth-derived products, a direct and material supply-chain risk for any manufacturer using magnets with trace Chinese content, including defense and EV supply chains.
insights.quote: In late 2025, China adopted its own version of the U.S. foreign direct product rule, asserting a right to decide whether companies can access magnets anywhere in the world if they contain even trace amounts of Chinese materials or were made using Chinese technology. In effect, Beijing turned against Washington the same extraterritorial tactic Washington had invented to control chips.

insights.claim: Over 55 percent of globally traded maize, wheat, rice, and soybeans pass through at least one maritime chokepoint, meaning energy disruptions can become food-price crises within weeks.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: A hard quantified link between energy chokepoint disruption and global food-price risk (55%+ of major staple crop trade transits chokepoints) — directly relevant to agricultural commodity and food-security investment risk modeling.
insights.quote: over 55 percent of globally traded maize, wheat, rice, and soybeans pass through at least one maritime chokepoint, and energy disruptions can become food-price crises within weeks.

insights.claim: Both Iran and the United States have suggested they intend to extract tolls from ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz, and other states could be tempted to start charging for access to international waterways more broadly.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: Flags an emerging monetization-of-chokepoints trend (toll extraction at Hormuz) that could set precedent for tolling at other global maritime chokepoints, raising global shipping and insurance costs structurally.
insights.quote: Both Iran and the United States have suggested they intend to extract tolls from ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz, and other states might be tempted to start charging for access to international waterways.

insights.claim: China already behaves as an 'artisan' state, advancing its interests by repurposing existing institutions (e.g., using the International Telecommunication Union to embed surveillance-friendly controls into global internet standards) and creating flexible new ones like the Shanghai Cooperation Organization and BRICS+ that are not intended to set global rules.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: Defines China's institutional strategy (flexible, repurposed, non-rule-setting coalitions) as the operative model for navigating an order-less world, a template that Western middle powers are urged to copy rather than continuing to pursue defunct multilateral 'architect' projects.
insights.quote: In many ways, China already behaves like an artisan state. It advances its interests by repurposing existing institutions, such as when it used the International Telecommunication Union to build surveillance-friendly controls into global Internet standards, and by creating new institutions, such as the Shanghai Cooperation Organization and BRICS+

insights.claim: Western middle powers continue to act like 'architects,' wasting effort on defunct projects such as Ireland and Spain's joining South Africa's genocide claim against Israel at the International Court of Justice, which has had virtually no effect on Israeli policy, and continued WTO tariff complaints against the U.S. that Leonard calls 'the equivalent of shouting into the void.'
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: Names specific recent multilateral-legalist efforts as effectively wasted diplomatic capital, a sharp critique relevant to assessing the practical impact of ongoing international legal actions (e.g., ICJ genocide proceedings, WTO tariff disputes) on actual policy outcomes.
insights.quote: Too many governments are still trying to curb conflicts using the UN or international courts. Ireland, for example, joined Spain in backing South Africa’s genocide claim against Israel at the International Court of Justice, a much-ballyhooed effort that has had virtually no effect on Israeli policy.

insights.claim: Leonard recommends that Europe and its allies pursue defensive chokepoint leverage of their own: Europe could ground more than half of China's commercial Airbus fleet by withholding software updates, and Taiwan could restrict its critical semiconductor industry to deter Chinese aggression against its sovereignty.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: Identifies specific, concrete leverage points (Airbus software, Taiwan semiconductors) middle powers could weaponize defensively — relevant to assessing the credibility and market impact of potential future European or Taiwanese retaliatory actions against China.
insights.quote: To protect itself from Chinese blackmail, Europe could leverage its Airbus sales by withholding software updates for China’s Airbus fleet, which would ground more than half of the country’s commercial planes... To deter China from threatening its sovereignty, Taiwan could restrict its critical semiconductor industry.

insights.claim: Leonard cites the UK's 2023 National Health Service contract awarding U.S. firm Palantir a major data platform, and a new British police AI program's interest in working with Palantir, as examples of the technological dependency Western states should instead offset by incentivizing domestic open-source providers and mandating open, portable data standards as a condition of public contracts.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: A concrete, named example (NHS-Palantir contract) of Western technological chokepoint dependency that Leonard argues should be avoided via procurement policy reform — relevant to assessing sovereign-tech and GovTech competitive dynamics in Europe.
insights.quote: In 2023, the United Kingdom’s National Health Service awarded the U.S. technology company Palantir a major contract to provide its new data platform; this year, a new British police AI program expressed interest in working with the firm. Instead, it should use the power of its purse to incentivize domestic providers
